facts.fact: The solar system is the Sun plus everything bound to it by gravity — eight planets, dwarf planets, moons, asteroids, comets and meteoroids.
The Nebular Hypothesis of the solar system is associated with Kant and Laplace.
The Sun and planets formed about 4.6 billion years ago.
About 99.9% of the nebular matter was pulled into the centre to form the Sun.
The terrestrial (inner) planets — Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars — are small, rocky and dense.
The Jovian (outer) planets — Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune — are large, gaseous and have many moons.
The asteroid belt lies between Mars and Jupiter.
One Astronomical Unit (AU), the mean Earth–Sun distance, is about 150 million km.
The Oort Cloud, a distant shell of icy bodies, is the source of long-period comets.
The Kuiper Belt beyond Neptune is home to Pluto.
Venus is the hottest planet because of the greenhouse effect of its thick CO2 atmosphere, though Mercury is closer to the Sun.
Venus rotates retrograde (clockwise, east to west), opposite to most planets.
A day on Venus (243 Earth days) is longer than its year (about 225 days).
Mars is called the Red Planet because of iron oxide on its surface.
Neptune has the strongest sustained winds of any planet, about 2,100 km/h.
Uranus spins on its side — its axis of rotation lies nearly in the plane of its orbit.
Jupiter is the largest planet; its moon Ganymede is the largest moon in the solar system.
Mercury is the smallest planet and the closest to the Sun.
Venus is called Earth's twin because of its similar size, mass and composition.
The solar system lies in the Milky Way, a barred-spiral galaxy.
Andromeda is the nearest major galaxy, about 2.5 million light-years away.
A light-year (about 9.46 trillion km) is a unit of distance, not time.
Proxima Centauri is the nearest star to the Sun, about 4.24 light-years away.
A dwarf planet fails only the IAU criterion of having cleared its orbital neighbourhood.
The IAU recognises five dwarf planets: Ceres, Pluto, Eris, Haumea and Makemake (Charon is a moon of Pluto).
A meteoroid is rock in space, a meteor the streak of light as it burns, a meteorite the piece that reaches the ground.
Comets have highly elliptical orbits, unlike the near-circular orbits of planets.
The Sun is about 75% hydrogen and 24% helium.
The Sun holds about 99.86% of the mass of the solar system.
Sunlight takes about 8 minutes 20 seconds to reach the Earth.
Sunspots are dark patches cooler than the surrounding surface.
The Sun's energy comes from nuclear fusion of hydrogen into helium in its core.
The Moon does not emit its own light; it reflects sunlight.
The phases of the Moon repeat about every 29 days.
The Moon formed from a giant impact — 'the big splat'.
A lunar eclipse occurs when the Earth comes between the Sun and Moon, only on a Full Moon.
A solar eclipse occurs when the Moon comes between the Sun and Earth, only on a New Moon.
An annular eclipse shows a 'ring of fire' because the Moon is near its farthest point and looks smaller than the Sun.
During a total solar eclipse the observer is within the Moon's umbra.
Eclipses are not monthly because the Moon's orbit is tilted about 5°; they need a new/full moon near a node.
Earth's axis is inclined at 66½° to its orbital plane, i.e. tilted 23½° from the vertical.
One rotation of the Earth takes about 24 hours and causes day and night.
The Earth rotates from west to east, so the Sun appears to rise in the east and set in the west.
The Earth revolves around the Sun in an elliptical orbit in 365¼ days.
The extra quarter day each year is collected into one extra day every four years — the leap year of 366 days.
On 21 June (summer solstice) the Sun is overhead at the Tropic of Cancer, giving the longest Northern Hemisphere day.
In the Northern Hemisphere the longest day normally occurs in the first half of June (21 June).
On 22 December (winter solstice) the Sun is overhead at the Tropic of Capricorn.
On the equinoxes, 21 March and 23 September, the Sun is overhead at the equator and day equals night everywhere.
On 21 June the Arctic Circle receives 24 hours of daylight (the Sun does not set there).
Seasons are caused by the Earth's axial tilt and revolution, not by its distance from the Sun.
The Earth is farthest from the Sun (aphelion) in early July, yet the Northern Hemisphere then has summer.
The Coriolis effect (Ferrel's Law) deflects moving objects to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern.
The Coriolis force is zero at the Equator and increases towards the poles.
The circle of illumination divides the lit and dark halves of the Earth and does not align with the axis because of the tilt.
Because of the tilt the poles get about six months of daylight and six months of darkness.
Geothermal energy, plate movements and the Earth's rotation and revolution bring dynamic changes to the Earth's surface (UPSC 2013).
Indian Standard Time is based on the 82½°E meridian.
One degree of latitude is about 111 km.
The Tropic of Cancer is at 23½°N and the Tropic of Capricorn at 23½°S.
The Arctic Circle is at 66½°N and the Antarctic Circle at 66½°S.
The Torrid Zone, the hottest heat zone, lies between the Tropic of Cancer and the Tropic of Capricorn.
The Temperate Zones lie between the tropics and the polar circles in each hemisphere.
The Frigid Zones lie north of the Arctic Circle and south of the Antarctic Circle.
The Prime Meridian (0°) passes through Greenwich and divides the Earth into Eastern and Western Hemispheres.
The Earth rotates 15° of longitude per hour, i.e. 1° in 4 minutes.
All places on the same meridian have the same local (solar) time.
The International Date Line broadly follows the 180° meridian.
IST is 5 hours 30 minutes ahead of GMT.
Places east of Greenwich are ahead of Greenwich time; places west are behind.
At 10:00 AM IST, the local time at Kohima (94°E) is about 10:46 AM (11½° × 4 min = 46 min ahead).
The Goldilocks (habitable) zone is the orbital band around a star where liquid water can exist — used in the search for Earth-like planets.
Earth's magnetic field has reversed its polarity many times over geological time.
Living organisms modified the early atmosphere; the early atmosphere had no free oxygen.
The Pole Star (Polaris) lies nearly above Earth's axis of rotation, so it appears fixed and marks north.
The Iron Catastrophe was the heating of the young Earth to iron's melting point, letting iron and nickel sink to form the core.
The Great Oxidation Event, about 2.4 billion years ago, was the rise of free oxygen from early photosynthesis.
The Saros cycle, after which similar eclipses repeat, is about 18 years 11 days (8 hours).
Astronomy, the study of celestial objects, is one of the oldest sciences; ancient Indians used it for calendars, festivals and sowing.
The Observable Universe is the spherical region of the universe that can be observed from Earth.
The Big Bang took place about 13.7 billion years ago.
Edwin Hubble provided evidence in 1920 that the universe is expanding.
Georges Lemaître proposed the Big Bang idea.
The Steady State theory of the universe is associated with Fred Hoyle.
Laplace revised Kant's nebular hypothesis in 1796.
The Planetesimal Hypothesis (1900) was given by Chamberlin and Moulton — a passing star pulled material from the Sun.
Sir James Jeans and later Sir Harold Jeffreys supported the passing-star (tidal) idea.
Otto Schmidt and Carl Weizsacker revised the nebular hypothesis (1950).
The Milky Way is called Akash Ganga in India.
The solar nebula began collapsing some 5–5.6 billion years ago, probably triggered by a nearby supernova.
Only 0.1% of the nebular matter stayed in orbit as a flat protoplanetary disc, where the planets formed.
Accretion built planetesimals, which grew into proto-planets and then planets.
About 500 million years after formation, the young Earth reached iron's melting point of about 1,538°C.
The sinking of heavy iron and nickel to the core while light silicates stayed outside is called planetary differentiation.
The Earth formed about 4.5–4.54 billion years ago.
The Sun's diameter is about 1.4 million km, about 109 times that of the Earth.
The Sun's layers from inside out are the core, radiative zone, convective zone, photosphere, chromosphere and corona.
The photosphere is the Sun's visible surface, from which light is emitted.
The chromosphere is seen as a red ring during a solar eclipse.
The corona is the Sun's outermost layer, seen as a halo during a total solar eclipse.
Sunspots are 500–1,500°C cooler than their surroundings, and the Sun is about 1% cooler during sunspot activity.
The solar wind is a stream of charged particles (electrons and protons) flowing from the Sun at up to 900 km/s at about 1 million °C.
Solar flares are bursts of energy from magnetic anomalies that heat the corona to 10–20 million °C.
Solar prominences are large arcs of gas held by the Sun's magnetic fields that often erupt into space.
The Sun is about 5 billion years old, in the middle of its life, with about 5 billion more years to shine.
At the end of its life the Sun will become a red giant and then leave a white dwarf.
Aditya-L1, India's solar mission (launched 2 September 2023 from Sriharikota), observes the Sun from Lagrange point L1, about 1.5 million km away.
The planets in order from the Sun are Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune.
Indian names: Budh (Mercury), Shukra (Venus), Mangal (Mars), Brihaspati (Jupiter), Shani (Saturn), Arun (Uranus), Varun (Neptune).
Earth is the densest planet (5.51 g/cm³).
Saturn is the least dense planet (0.69 g/cm³) — it would float on water.
Mercury has the shortest year — 88 Earth days.
Jupiter spins fastest (one rotation in about 9.9 hours), making it an oblate spheroid.
Venus has the slowest rotation (243 Earth days).
Neptune takes about 164.8 Earth years to orbit the Sun — the longest year.
Revolution periods: Venus 225 days, Mars 687 days, Jupiter 11.86 years, Saturn 29.46 years, Uranus 84 years.
Mercury and Venus have no moons.
Mars has two moons, Phobos and Deimos.
Saturn now has the most moons (274 recognised in 2025); the source table lists Jupiter 95 and Saturn 82.
Venus and Uranus are the two planets that rotate east to west (clockwise).
Mercury, with almost no atmosphere, ranges from about 427°C by day to −173°C at night — the widest diurnal range.
Mercury is smaller than Ganymede and Titan but has more mass than both.
Venus is the brightest planet, third-brightest object after the Sun and Moon, with the highest albedo from sulphuric acid clouds.
Venus's atmosphere is about 96% carbon dioxide with a surface pressure 92 times that of Earth.
Venus is seen as the morning star and the evening star.
Mars has no surface liquid water because its atmospheric pressure is under 1% of Earth's, though landforms show water once existed.
Mars lost its magnetosphere about 4 billion years ago, so the solar wind strips its ionosphere.
Mars's air is about 96% CO2, 1.93% argon and 1.89% nitrogen; methane has been detected.
Olympus Mons on Mars is the highest volcano in the solar system.
Jupiter's four Galilean moons — Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto — were discovered by Galileo.
Jupiter's Great Red Spot is a giant storm in its banded atmosphere.
Saturn's rings are made of billions of particles of ice and ice-covered rock.
Titan (Saturn) is the second-largest moon and the only moon with a substantial atmosphere, mostly nitrogen.
Ganymede is 5,268 km across; the Earth's Moon (3,474 km) is the fifth-largest moon.
Uranus and Neptune are the ice giants — the twins of the outer solar system — rich in water, ammonia and methane ices.
A planet is a celestial body moving in an elliptical orbit around a star.
In 2006 the IAU (meeting at Prague) defined a planet and reclassified Pluto as a dwarf planet.
An IAU planet orbits the Sun, is round (hydrostatic equilibrium), is not a satellite, and has cleared its orbit.
Pluto (2,377 km) and Eris (2,326 km) are similar-sized Kuiper Belt dwarf planets.
Ceres (946 km) is the largest asteroid, a proto-planet and a dwarf planet in the asteroid belt.
The asteroid belt is a remnant that failed to form a planet because of Jupiter's gravitational interference.
Asteroids are made of refractory rocky and metallic minerals.
The Kuiper Belt extends from Neptune's orbit at 30 AU to 50 AU and may be treated as the extent of the Solar System.
Near the Sun a comet's nucleus outgasses to form a coma and a tail.
A comet's tail always points away from the Sun.
Halley's Comet returns about every 76 years; it last appeared in 1986 and is next due in 2061.
Meteors are called shooting stars, but they are pieces of rock, not stars.
A meteor shower is seen when the Earth passes through a comet's tail (debris).
The Moon shows eight major phases.
In the waxing phase the Moon grows; in the waning phase it shrinks.
A Blue Moon is the second full moon in a single calendar month.
Diwali is celebrated on New Moon day.
Guru Nanak Jayanti is celebrated on Full Moon day.
Maha Shivratri falls on a night of the waning moon (13th/14th night).
Eid-ul-Fitr is celebrated on the day after the crescent moon is sighted.
The Moon's surface is barren and dusty with craters and high mountains, and it has no atmosphere.
Chandrayaan-1 (2008) detected water molecules on the Moon, though it has no liquid water.
The Moon-forming impactor (Theia) was one to three times the size of Mars; the Moon formed about 4.44 billion years ago.
The Moon is about 384,400 km from the Earth.
The Moon rotates once per orbit, so the same face always faces the Earth.
The sidereal month (one orbit) is about 27.3 days; the synodic month (phase cycle) about 29.5 days.
Neil Armstrong, followed by Edwin Aldrin, first landed on the Moon on 21 July 1969 (Apollo 11).
Chandrayaan-3 was launched on 14 July 2023 from the Satish Dhawan Space Centre, Sriharikota (Andhra Pradesh).
Chandrayaan-3 entered lunar orbit on 5 August 2023 and landed near the lunar south pole on 23 August 2023.
The three types of lunar eclipse are total, partial and penumbral.
In a total lunar eclipse the Moon often turns red — a 'blood moon' — as Earth's atmosphere scatters sunlight onto it.
A lunar eclipse is visible from anywhere on the night side of the Earth, a solar eclipse only where the Moon's shadow falls.
The three types of solar eclipse are total, partial and annular.
The corona becomes visible during a total solar eclipse.
Stars are celestial bodies of hot gases, mainly hydrogen and helium, that emit their own light.
Ursa Major (Great Bear / Saptarishi / Big Dipper) has seven main stars — three in the handle and four in the bowl.
Merak and Dubhe, the pointer stars of Ursa Major, point to the Pole Star.
Orion (the Hunter) has a belt of three stars in a line with four stars in a quadrilateral.
Sirius is the brightest star in the night sky; a line through Orion's belt points to it (it lies in Canis Major).
Cassiopeia, seen in northern winter, is shaped like a W.
Leo Major is visible from both hemispheres and appears upside down in the Southern Hemisphere.
A constellation is a group of stars forming a recognisable pattern; its stars may be at very different distances.
The Earth's shape is a geoid — flattened at the poles and bulging at the equator.
Earth's equatorial diameter is about 12,756 km and its polar diameter about 12,714 km.
A sidereal day is 23 hours 56 minutes 4 seconds; a solar day is 24 hours.
A point on the equator moves at about 1,670 km/h because of rotation.
The Earth revolves around the Sun at about 30 km per second.
A century year is a leap year only if divisible by 400 (2000 was, 1900 was not); February then has 29 days.
Seasonal variation in the length of day and night is due to the Earth's revolution on a tilted axis (UPSC 2013).
At the equator day and night are about 12 hours each throughout the year.
'Equinox' comes from Latin aequi (equal) + noctium (night).
'Solstice' comes from Latin sol (sun) + stitium (standing still).
On the June solstice the subsolar point is at 23.5°N, on the December solstice at 23.5°S; at the equinoxes the Sun is at 90° over the equator.
In the Northern Hemisphere 21 March is the vernal (spring) equinox and 23 September the autumnal equinox.
On 22 December the Antarctic Circle receives 24 hours of daylight.
The Earth is nearest the Sun (perihelion, about 147 million km) around 3 January.
Twilight is shortest at the equator and longest at the poles.
Latitude is denoted by the Greek letter phi (φ) and longitude by lambda (λ).
There are 179 parallels of latitude (including the equator) and 360 meridians of longitude.
One degree of latitude is about 110.6 km at the equator and 111.7 km at the poles.
Meridians are semicircles whose spacing decreases polewards, becoming zero at the poles.
Parallels of latitude decrease in size away from the equator.
The Prime Meridian through Greenwich was adopted at the International Meridian Conference of 1884.
Latitudes are used to classify temperature zones; longitudes to classify time zones.
The International Date Line zigzags to avoid dividing land and island groups.
Crossing the International Date Line westward a day is gained (date advances); eastward a day is repeated.
The Earth is divided into 24 time zones of one hour, each about 15° of longitude wide.
Russia has 11 standard times.
France holds the record for the most time zones — 12.
Local time at Dwarka (Gujarat) and Dibrugarh (Assam) differs by about 1 hour 45 minutes.
The IST meridian 82°30'E passes near Mirzapur in Uttar Pradesh.
When it is 2:00 pm in London, it is 7:30 pm in India.
India extends from about 68°7'E to 97°25'E — about 30° of longitude, i.e. about 2 hours of local time.
The 82°30'E meridian passes through Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Odisha and Andhra Pradesh.
Andhra Pradesh lies about 12°37'N–19°54'N, wholly in the Torrid Zone south of the Tropic of Cancer.
The Tropic of Cancer passes through eight Indian states: Gujarat, Rajasthan, MP, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, West Bengal, Tripura and Mizoram.
